report:
### Conclusion
Your impression is correct: high-quality evidence demonstrates that **knee arthroscopy (joint endoscopy) does not effectively help with osteoarthritis of the knee joint**.

### Key Evidence

1. **No Superiority to Placebo:** A landmark randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* established that arthroscopic lavage and debridement provided no greater pain relief or functional improvement than a sham (placebo) procedure (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259).
2. **No Added Benefit Over Conservative Care:** A subsequent trial in *The New England Journal of Medicine* demonstrated that adding arthroscopic surgery to optimized physical therapy and medical treatment yielded no additional benefit over physical therapy and medication alone (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).
3. **Clinical Practice Guidelines:**
   - A *BMJ* clinical practice guideline issued a strong recommendation against arthroscopic knee surgery in nearly all patients with degenerative knee disease, noting that it provides no meaningful clinical benefit (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982).
   - American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) guidelines do not recommend routine arthroscopy with lavage or debridement for patients with a primary diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis (https://scispace.com/papers/a-review-of-2021-and-2022-aaos-guidelines-for-meniscal-50ox5zjpmc).

In summary, major clinical trials and clinical practice guidelines consistently show that arthroscopy is ineffective for managing knee osteoarthritis compared to non-surgical care or placebo procedures.
